Chapter 2: Government Policies and the Shaping of a New Society
When you think about post-war migration to Australia, it’s impossible to separate the story from the government policies and attitudes that shaped that era. Right after the war, Australia was at a crossroads. The country needed to grow its population—and fast—but also wanted to hold onto a sense of who it was.
So, what did the government do? At first, they decided to focus on bringing in migrants from Britain and other English-speaking countries. The idea was pretty simple: people who spoke the same language and shared similar customs would blend in more easily, helping Australia maintain its identity.
But the world was changing in ways nobody could ignore. With so many people displaced by the war and Australia itself facing shortages of workers, the old plan just didn’t work anymore. That’s when the doors began to open wider—to Italians, Greeks, Poles, Yugoslavs, and many others from all across Europe.
Each new group arrived with its own unique story, its own reasons for leaving home, and dreams for the future.
Now, the government’s approach was a mix of practicality and, honestly, a bit of old-fashioned paternalism. New arrivals were often assigned to specific jobs and places to live, sometimes with little say in the matter. There was a big push to “assimilate”—to encourage migrants to pick up Australian customs and language as quickly as possible.
Imagine getting official pamphlets and orientation sessions on everything from hygiene to social do’s and don’ts—sometimes in ways that felt a little patronizing or just out of touch.
For many migrants, this mix of support and control was both a blessing and a source of frustration. On one hand, there was housing, language classes, and help finding work—all things that made settling in a bit easier. On the other hand, it could feel like you were being managed by people who didn’t really understand your background or your dreams.
Some folks ended up working in factories or on construction sites, far from the careers they’d left behind. Others were sent out to rural areas, where homesickness and isolation sometimes hit the hardest.
But here’s where the story really gets interesting. Even with all these challenges, most newcomers found ways to adapt. In those hostels and workplaces, informal networks started to form. People shared tips about jobs, helped each other deal with the red tape, and offered a shoulder to lean on when times got tough.
Over time, these networks grew into real communities—places where old traditions could survive, even as new ones took root.
Not everything went according to plan, though. The push to assimilate sometimes backfired, leaving people feeling left out or even resented. In response, some migrants held on even tighter to their languages and customs, creating vibrant enclaves within Australian cities.
These communities became both a source of comfort for their members and, occasionally, a target for suspicion or worry about “foreign” influences.
As the years rolled by, it became obvious that integration was far messier—and far richer—than anyone had expected. Many migrants found ways to balance their old identities with their new lives, and in doing so, they helped transform Australia itself.
Food, music, and daily life began to reflect a growing diversity, even as debates about what it meant to belong continued.
So, if you look at government policy, it’s really a story of both guidance and limitation. Policy set the ground rules, but it couldn’t control what happened next.
The real building of a new society happened in the everyday moments—at kitchen tables, on job sites, in the neighborhoods and growing suburbs.
That’s where modern multicultural Australia truly began to take shape, in all its beautiful, unpredictable complexity.
